incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), Part 2, ss 12–19 (incorporation); s 190 (registered office); ss 128, 129 (board resolutions); s 152 (appointment of directors); Schedule 1 (default constitution); Regulations: Companies (Registers and Other Prescribed Information) Regulations 1995. Tax-exempt non-resident treatment for a New Zealand-incorporated International Company with foreign-sourced income is framed under Income Tax Act 2007, ss CW 9 and YB 4.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), Wellington, New Zealand
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Application for Registration of a New Zealand Company under s 12 of the Companies Act 1993 (lodged electronically via the New Zealand Companies Register Online Services portal)
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital is prescribed by New Zealand law; there is no escrow account requirement. The company may issue shares without fully paying them at incorporation, and no bank-controlled capital deposit is required. For International Company status, the beneficial ownership and management must remain non-resident and the company must derive no New Zealand-sourced income to preserve the tax-exempt treatment.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED THAT the Company adopt, without amendment, the constitution delivered to the Registrar of Companies upon incorporation, and that the directors confirm the validity of the registration application; RESOLVED THAT the registered office of the Company in New Zealand be and is hereby fixed at [street address, city, New Zealand], in accordance with s 190 of the Companies Act 1993, and that the Registrar of Companies be authorized to record such address; RESOLVED THAT the Company issue and allot [number] ordinary shares at an issue price of NZ$[amount] per share to the subscribers named in the application, and that the directors be and are hereby authorized to issue share certificates and enter the allottees in the share register; RESOLVED THAT [full name] be and is hereby appointed a director of the Company, to hold office pursuant to the constitution and s 152 of the Companies Act 1993; RESOLVED THAT [full name] be and is hereby appointed Chief Executive Officer of the Company with authority to manage the day-to-day affairs of the Company; RESOLVED THAT [full name] be and is hereby appointed Company Secretary and that [full name] be appointed as the authorized representative for non-resident corporate administration matters; RESOLVED THAT the directors be and are hereby authorized to open bank accounts, sign contracts and leases, obtain any non-sectoral operating certifications required for physical premises, and execute all ancillary instruments necessary to give effect to these resolutions; RESOLVED THAT the minutes of this meeting, signed by the chair, be placed in the Company's minute book and that an electronic copy be archived at the registered office.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Company Name Availability Search and Reservation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Online Services (Register of Companies)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Search the Companies Register to confirm that the proposed corporate name is not identical or confusingly similar to any existing name in New Zealand and does not breach the restrictions in s 14 of the Companies Act 1993. Submit an online name reservation application for the proposed International Company name. The reservation is valid for 20 working days from confirmation, unless extended. Provide the overseas parent or founder's identity and the intended New Zealand registered agent details for the reservation.
required_dossiers: Proposed company name in Latin script
Consent letter from the proposed New Zealand registered agent
Identification and contact details of the applicant/subscriber
Proof of corporate existence and current name of any overseas parent company, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar declines the name under s 14, file a written submission seeking reconsideration within 20 working days of the refusal notice, accompanied by evidence of distinguishability or prior authorization. Alternatively, reserve a revised name or apply to the Registrar for an exemption in accordance with the Companies Act 1993 and the Companies (Name Availability) Rules.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation of Constitution, Subscriber Statement, and Statutory Consents
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (pre-lodgement review / registered agent)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the written constitution of the International Company, or elect expressly that the default company constitution set out in Schedule 1 of the Companies Act 1993 shall apply. The constitution must comply with the Companies Act 1993 including restrictions on board powers, shareholder rights, share transfer, and director indemnities. Obtain signed subscriber consent forms, director consent forms, and a precise notice of the registered office and an address for service in New Zealand. If single-member incorporation is used, record the sole subscriber's resolution authorizing the registration.
required_dossiers: Memorandum or deed of constitution (optional but recommended)
Subscription statement listing initial shareholders and share allocations
Consent to act as director (s 151, Companies Act 1993)
Consent to act as company secretary, if any
Notice of registered office in New Zealand
Notice of address for service
Powers of attorney or board resolution of the ultimate overseas parent entity
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar or the registered agent returns the documents due to incompleteness, cure the query by correcting the inconsistent signatures, amending the constitution to include required content, or re-executing the consent forms within 10 working days. A signed affidavit of correctness may be required for any documentary defect.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Electronic Lodgement of the Application for Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, Online Services
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Log on to the New Zealand Companies Register, select 'Register a Company', and complete the statutory application form under s 12 of the Companies Act 1993. Attach the signed constitution (if applicable), subscriber details, director details, registered office address, address for service, and the name reservation reference number. Pay the prescribed incorporation fee by credit card or bank transfer. Upon successful validation, the system generates a provisional registration number and submits the documents to the Registrar.
required_dossiers: Completed statutory incorporation application
Constitution or election to use Schedule 1 default constitution
Directors' consents and ethical/eligibility declarations
Notice of registered office and address for service
Name reservation confirmation reference
Certified copies of identity documents for all directors and shareholders
Payment of official incorporation fee
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried or placed in rejection, review the Registrar's deficiency notice and submit amendments through the same portal within 15 working days. If refused, request a formal reconsideration under s 14B of the Companies Act 1993 or file a fresh application with corrected particulars. Judicial review of an adverse decision is possible in the High Court of New Zealand.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Issuance of Certificate of Incorporation and New Zealand Business Number (NZBN)
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office; New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) Registrar
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Once the Registrar is satisfied, the company is incorporated by the issue of a Certificate of Incorporation under s 17 of the Companies Act 1993, and a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) is automatically allocated. The certificate and NZBN are transmitted electronically through the Online Services portal. Verify that the company name, director details, registered office, and any constitution are recorded exactly as submitted. The company must immediately obtain certified copies of the certificate and keep them at its registered office.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
NZBN notification letter
Final constitution as registered
Register of directors and shareholders extracted from the Companies Register
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If there is an error in the certificate or register, submit an online 'Application to Correct a Register' under s 360 of the Companies Act 1993, or file a notice of change of particulars. In urgent cases, apply to the Registrar for an expedited correction; in case of refusal, the High Court may order rectification of the register.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Board Meeting and Corporate Governance Implementation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the Company (meeting may be held at the registered office or by video conference)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first meeting of the directors following incorporation. Adopt the pro forma First Board Resolution, approve the allotment of shares, appoint the directors, executive officers, and company secretary, approve the registered office address, authorize opening of bank accounts, and approve any leases or service agreements for the physical premises. Record minutes of all resolutions and include them in the company's minute book. File any changes of particulars with the Companies Office within 20 working days, including appointment of directors, registered office changes, and director shareholdings.
required_dossiers: Notice of first board meeting
Board resolution adopting the constitution
Board resolution approving share subscription and allotment
Consents and appointments of directors and officers
Minutes of first board meeting
Lease agreement or proof of physical registered office address
Bank account mandate documents (for post-formation banking)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If an appointment or share allotment is found to be procedurally defective, the directors may pass a subsequent ratification resolution under s 33 and s 128 of the Companies Act 1993. A void or irregular allotment can be corrected by a special resolution of shareholders and an online notice of correction submitted to the Companies Office.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Establishment of Statutory Registers and Ongoing Governance Compliance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Directors and the New Zealand registered agent acting on behalf of the International Company
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare and maintain the statutory registers required by the Companies Act 1993: the share register, register of directors and company secretaries, register of charges, minutes book of shareholder and board proceedings, and the register of issued transfers. Ensure the annual return timeline is scheduled with the Companies Office. Adopt the internal corporate governance policies, including non-resident board procedures, conflict-of-interest management, and a resolution framework for the International Company to preserve its tax-exempt status. The registered agent shall archive executed resolutions and register updates at the company's address for service.
required_dossiers: Share register confirming initial allotments
Register of directors with names, addresses, dates of appointment
Register of charges and encumbrances, if any
Minute book containing first board resolutions and future resolutions
Annual return calendar and Companies Office reminders
Corporate governance and conflicts-of-interest policy manuals
Certificate of Incorporation as posted at the registered office
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar identifies a statutory register deficiency, file a rectification statement and, where necessary, apply to the High Court for an order to correct the register. Directors may be liable for continued non-compliance; remedy by obtaining the company secretary's verification, updating the register, and filing the correct notice of change of particulars.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: No sector-specific industrial licensing authority exists for international media relations and crisis public relations services under ISIC 7310 / NAICS 541820 in New Zealand. For physical premises and workplace matters, the competent authorities are the territorial authority (city/district council) and the Building Department of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE).
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not Applicable - No Statutory Occupational License for Public Relations Agency Operations; Non-sectoral Business Activity Endorsement may be required from the local territorial authority for physical premises and any signage

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Authority New Zealand (EPA); local territorial councils for land-use and discharge consents
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt - Full EIA not required for an office-based public relations and communications firm. Only a limited land-use / building consent is triggered if physical premises are altered; any generator or emergency fuel storage would require a resource consent. Activities are otherwise classified as low-impact and exempt under the Resource Management Act 1991 and the Resource Management (National Environmental Standards for Air Quality) Regulations 2004.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: For office-based PR operations, no point-source wastewater or VOC discharge is expected. Where any catering, printing, or small mechanical plant is used, all wastewater trade waste discharges must comply with the relevant territorial authority's trade-waste bylaw, and any dry-cleaning or printing solvent emissions must remain below the permitted VOC thresholds of the National Environmental Standards for Air Quality (Tables 2 and 3). Waste handling must comply with the Waste Minimisation Act 2008 and local waste management plans.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: The company must obtain a Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) for the office premises if the building hosts specified systems (fire alarms, sprinklers, air-conditioning, emergency lighting, or lifts). A fire evacuation procedure, means-of-escape certification, and safety signage in compliance with the Building Act 2004 and the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 are required. Before occupation, the tenant must procure structural, electrical, and plumbing compliance statements from the building owner, and file a 'Form 12A - Change of Building Use or Extension of Building Life' if the use changes occupancy. There is no civil-defence clearance specific to a public relations firm, but emergency preparedness and evacuation arrangements must be documented and exercised annually.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department of New Zealand (Inland Revenue / Te Tari Tāke); official taxpayer portal: myIR Secure Online Services (myir.ird.govt.nz) and public information portal www.ird.govt.nz
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A non-resident offshore International Company (CK_IC) that has any New Zealand GST-registrable activity must first obtain a New Zealand IRD number. Procedure: (1) file Form IR596 'Application for IRD number for a non-resident company' with Inland Revenue, attaching the certificate of incorporation, constitutional documents, board resolutions, and identification of directors and ultimate shareholders; (2) upon IRD number issuance, apply for GST registration either online through myIR or by filing Form IR356 'GST registration form', selecting the correct filing frequency (monthly, two-monthly, or six-monthly); (3) if the company carries on a taxable activity wholly outside New Zealand, GST registration is voluntary only when below the NZD 60,000 taxable-supplies threshold and compulsory when that threshold is exceeded; (4) obtain an NZBN (New Zealand Business Number) only if creating a local establishment, which is not required for pure offshore service operations; (5) appointing a New Zealand agent or tax adviser is not statutorily mandatory but is recommended for myIR credentials and service of notice, because the branch/agent may be treated as the company's representative for tax administration purposes.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Tax_Exempt_Zone: The CK_IC is classified as a non-resident exempt offshore International Company. It is outside the scope of New Zealand income tax on all foreign-source income provided its centre of effective management is outside New Zealand, it derives no New Zealand-sourced income, and it does not maintain a New Zealand permanent establishment (ss. YD 2 and YD 4, Income Tax Act 2007). The company has no New Zealand entity-level income tax liability while the exempt-zone conditions are continuously satisfied. For indirect tax purposes, it is not subject to New Zealand GST on supplies made wholly outside New Zealand, but it may have GST registration and return obligations to the extent it makes taxable supplies in or from New Zealand (for example, remote services provided to New Zealand-resident consumers or non-zero-rated supplies to New Zealand businesses).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate a US-style check-the-box election. The available classification elections and provisions are: (1) Look-Through Company (LTC) election under Subpart HB, Income Tax Act 2007, available only to close companies with five or fewer shareholders, causing tax transparency while retaining limited liability; (2) grandfathered Qualifying Company (QC) status for companies that elected before the 2010 regime closure (no new QC elections permitted); (3) voluntary GST registration election under s. 51, GST Act 1985, available to any person carrying on a taxable activity, including non-residents; (4) the GST land zero-rating election based on taxable-use percentage under ss. 11(1)(mb) and 78C, GST Act 1985; (5) hybrid and branch mismatch rule-ordering positions under Subpart FH, Income Tax Act 2007, whereby a taxpayer may elect which mismatch rule applies to a cross-border structure; and (6) application for a private binding ruling under Part 5A, Tax Administration Act 1994, to confirm the zero-rating or offshore treatment of a specific international PR retainer arrangement.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 (New Zealand), administered by Inland Revenue
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in any continuous 12-month period (general statutory threshold and the threshold applicable to non-resident offshore suppliers of remote services). Effective 1 April 2025, the NZD 60,000 registration threshold has been removed for offshore suppliers of remote services and low-value goods supplied to New Zealand consumers, making GST registration compulsory for all such offshore suppliers regardless of turnover.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand does not impose mandatory electronic invoicing, real-time fiscal clearance, or digital stamping. GST returns are filed electronically via myIR on Form GST101 using a monthly, two-monthly, or six-monthly cycle, without government pre-clearance of individual invoices. Voluntary Peppol-based interoperable e-invoicing has been adopted through the NZ e-Invoice framework for B2B transactions, and New Zealand Customs uses the Trade Single Window / CDEX platform for export declarations. A taxpayer claiming zero-rating must nevertheless retain full substantiation of the export or offshore service supply, including tax invoices that meet the requirements of ss. 24 and 24B, GST Act 1985, with foreign-currency amounts and exchange-rate calculations properly documented.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating at 0% GST is available under s. 11(1), GST Act 1985. For goods: the goods must be exported by the supplier within 28 days of the time of supply (s. 11(1)(a)). For services: services are zero-rated if supplied to a person who is non-resident and is outside New Zealand at the time the services are performed (s. 11(1)(c)), subject to exceptions for services supplied in connection with New Zealand land, goods in New Zealand, or services physically performed in New Zealand. For the overseas PR and communications firm, international media relations, crisis PR, and advisory retainer services provided to offshore non-resident clients outside New Zealand qualify for zero-rating under s. 11(1)(c). Remote digital deliverables supplied to a New Zealand GST-registered recipient may be zero-rated only where the B2B conditions in s. 11(1)(mb) are satisfied and the recipient acquires the services for the principal purpose of making taxable supplies; otherwise, 15% GST applies.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (export entry lodged electronically through the New Zealand Customs Service Trade Single Window, evidencing physical export of goods within 28 days of supply and matching the GST zero-rating claim)

Bill of Lading or Air Waybill (transport document evidencing the goods left New Zealand and the overseas destination; for a pure services firm, this may be replaced by the executed retainer agreement, service delivery reports, and time logs demonstrating delivery to an offshore client)

Inward Remittance Certificate (bank-issued certificate or remittance advice from a New Zealand registered bank evidencing receipt of the foreign currency proceeds from the overseas client within the mandated repatriation window)

Commercial invoice and inter-party service agreement (contractual documentation establishing the non-resident status of the recipient, the place of performance, and the arm's-length pricing of the PR retainer for audit substantiation)
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue subjects export zero-rating claims and GST refunds to heightened audit scrutiny, particularly for services exporters and offshore-registered entities. Under the Tax Administration Act 1994, a tax shortfall arising from evasion or an intent to mislead attracts a civil penalty of 150% of the shortfall; an abusive tax position attracts 100%; gross carelessness attracts 40%; and late filing and non-payment penalties accrue in addition to use-of-money interest on unpaid or over-claimed GST. Fraudulent or unsupported zero-rating claims, including false inward remittance certificates, fabricated bills of lading, or fictitious offshore service contracts, trigger retrospective reassessment, because the four-year limitation period does not apply in cases of fraud or misrepresentation, and result in immediate GST refund clawback, deregistration or disqualification from voluntary registration, and criminal prosecution. Conviction carries fines of up to NZD 50,000 for an individual and NZD 250,000 for a company, with imprisonment of up to five years for tax evasion. Directors, shadow directors, and any New Zealand agent who aided the false claim may be held jointly and severally liable for the tax shortfall, penalties, and interest.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua) — the statutory central bank and prudential regulator for the New Zealand banking system, responsible for monetary policy, bank licensing, and the settlement ultimate, and the de facto administrator of New Zealand's open foreign-exchange regime (New Zealand abolished statutory exchange controls in 1984 and no group of the Minister of Finance or the Reserve Bank exercises exchange-control approval powers). The Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) — the home-state offshore regulator for the Cook Islands International Company (CK_IC), administering the International Companies Act 2010-2011 and supervising the registered agent, but not a central bank. The New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) administers financial sanctions and asset-freeze lists that bind all reporting entities.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The New Zealand Dollar (NZD) is fully convertible on both current-account and capital-account transactions. There are no surrender requirements, no mandatory conversion ratios, no exchange-control permits, and no limitation on profit remittance, dividend distribution, branch repatriation, or liquidation proceeds for residents or non-residents. The Cook Islands operates in practice under the same open regime: NZD is legal tender in the Cook Islands, the Cook Islands dollar (CKD) is pegged at par with NZD and does not create a conversion barrier, and a CK_IC may hold and freely deploy NZD, USD, EUR, AUD, GBP and any other acceptable currency in accounts in New Zealand or abroad. The only profit-remittance hurdle is a tax compliance overlay, not an FX restriction: outbound income distributions sourced from New Zealand may attract non-resident withholding tax (NRWT), which is settled through the banking system and does not require central-bank approval. For capital-account flows, inbound shareholder loans and equity injections require no RBNZ consent, but must be classified accurately for bank reporting, CRS/FATCA disclosures, and the anti-money-laundering travel rule applicable to all cross-border wire transfers of NZD 1,000 or above.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Neither New Zealand nor the Cook Islands imposes export-proceeds surrender rules, statutory repatriation timelines, or mandatory conversion ratios. Receipts for international media relations, crisis communications, and overseas PR retainer services may be retained in the foreign currency of receipt (including USD ACH collections from US clients), held in offshore foreign-currency accounts, swept to the New Zealand operating account at the corporate's election, or redeployed directly to settle trade disbursements. New Zealand's Overseas Investment Act 2005 and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 impose no exhaustion requirements on export or service receipts, but do require reporting entities to submit prescribed transaction reports (e.g., large-value cash and cross-border wire reports) to the New Zealand Financial Intelligence Unit, and every wire transfer must carry complete originator and beneficiary information under the domestic travel-rule regulations.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational NZD Treasury Account (primary settlement and liquidity account)
Capital Escrow Account (NZD) plus USD Foreign Currency Account (FCY) for segregated client retainer escrow
Outbound Trade Settlement Account (multi-currency USD/AUD/EUR) for SWIFT MT103 and commercial LC disbursements
Retainer ACH Receivables Account (through US correspondent banking channel)
Operational NZD Account (non-essential backup or secondary treasury account)

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility Rating: MEDIUM-LOW, with bank-grade EMIs outranking consumer-oriented platforms. Regulated cross-border fintech EMIs legally permitted to onboard a Cook Islands International Company under the AML/CFT Act 2009 include Airwallex (Australian ADI-regulated and NZ FSP-registered), Currenxie (UK FCA-registered EMI), Payoneer, Deel, and Wise. In practice, Wise Business is the least viable because its licensing terms generally require the entity's registered jurisdiction to align with the account country, a condition the CK_IC cannot satisfy without also registering an NZ branch; Payoneer accepts the structure only with a live operating website, signed media contracts, and a director video call; Currenxie demonstrates tolerance for Pacific offshore companies but imposes a strict beneficial-ownership declaration. Airwallex is the most viable digital EMI: it accepts Cook Islands ICs carrying an FSC Certificate of Eligibility, provides virtual NZD and USD accounts, enables US ACH inbound collections, and routes outbound MT103-equivalent SWIFT payments. Legal constraint: any NZ-licensed EMI must apply a risk-based approach; the tax-exempt status of the CK_IC is not a prohibition, but the EMI must obtain a sealed extract of the confidential beneficial-ownership register from the Cook Islands registered agent, a New Zealand physical service address (a registered agent office or PO Box is rejected), and an executed customer due-diligence file before opening virtual accounts. Cross-border digital EMIs with no physical presence in New Zealand are not permitted to onboard the CK_IC without obtaining a Financial Service Provider (FSP) registration under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Statutory mandate: none. The AML/CFT Act 2009 and the AML/CFT Regulations 2011 do not require directors or beneficial owners of a CK_IC to appear physically at an executive branch; remote onboarding is legally compliant where identity verification is performed through (i) a licensed digital identity service provider under the Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Act 2023, or (ii) certification by an independent suitably qualified person — a New Zealand solicitor, chartered accountant, or a Cook Islands notary public — who has met the individual face-to-face or via an equivalent verification channel, followed by a live video-conference interview with the bank's relationship team. In current NZ major-bank practice, remote account opening for a Cook Islands International Company is achievable within 10-15 business days under the following protocol: (1) each director, shareholder, and the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) holding 25% or more submits a notarially certified passport and proof-of-address obtained within the last six months; (2) the IC's authorised signatories complete a video interview with the bank's corporate onboarding unit; (3) the Cook Islands registered agent issues a compliance certificate via the FSC-licensed channel confirming the non-public registers and the absence of bearer shares (unless expressly disclosed); and (4) if any UBO is a citizen or resident of a higher-risk jurisdiction, the bank may require an in-person biometric attendance at an Auckland, Wellington, or Christchurch branch. A fully paper-based file without any interview is not accepted by any New Zealand tier-1 bank in the current risk environment.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Offshore-vehicle red flag: the CK_IC is a Cook Islands 'Tax-Exempt Zone' international company, which creates a presumption of preferential tax treatment, opacity, or potential non-compliance with New Zealand'ss anti-tax-avoidance standards.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: FSC Certificate of Compliance; Certificate of Incorporation; Cook Islands International Companies Act 2010-2011 tax exemption certificate; a legal opinion from Cook Islands counsel confirming the IC is not an interposed or asset-concealment vehicle; OECD CRS / New Zealand AEOI self-certification for the UBO; the IC's consolidated financial statements and a 3-year business plan of the overseas PR and media-relations agency; a declaration of economic substance showing physical offices, employees, or contracted professionals in the Cook Islands or New Zealand; and a tax-residence analysis confirming where central management and control is exercised.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial-ownership opacity: a Cook Islands IC maintains non-public registers of directors, shareholders, and beneficial owners, so the onboarding bank cannot independently verify UBOs through public registries.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: A sealed extract of the Statutory Confidential Register of Beneficial Owners issued by the Cook Islands registered agent to the bank; a fully completed AML/CFT section 31 customer declaration naming each UBO and their natural-person identifiers; the IC's trust deed, shareholders' agreement, and any power-of-attorney instruments; and an original compliance certificate from the registered agent under FSC AML Rules confirming the adequacy of the underlying CDD file.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border round-tripping and media-industry exposure: the PR agency pays journalists, media outlets, and sub-agents in multiple jurisdictions, triggering concerns about undue client payments, unexplained commissions, or sanctions-list hits in the media supply chain.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Signed client retainer contracts and standard form engagement letters; itemised invoices for media purchasing, crisis-response retainers, and freelance journalist contributions; a sanctions and PEP screening log evidencing that each counterparty is screened against OFAC, the NZ consolidated list, the EU consolidated list, and United Nations Security Council lists before disbursement; internal policies prohibiting payments to shell media vendors; and 12 months of bank statements for the CK_IC demonstrating that fund flows match invoice timestamps and values.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: US ACH retainer collection without US tax or corporate transparency disclosure: the 'Retainer_ACH' stream originates from US clients, prompting the bank to enquire whether the IC is 'doing business' in the United States, is subject to the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) beneficial-ownership information reporting, or has undisclosed US reporting obligations.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: A US federal tax opinion confirming that the CK_IC has no US permanent establishment or effectively connected income solely by virtue of receiving retainer payments via ACH; a FinCEN BOI-report exemption analysis (or a copy of the filed BOI report if a US filing was made); a copy of the IC's independent contractor agreements with US clients excluding the creation of a US nexus; and an OFAC sanctions screen of every US payer routing funds through the ACH channel.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant protocol for equity and loan injections: (1) route funds from the investor's or parent's bank to the CK_IC's ANZ New Zealand Capital Escrow Account via SWIFT MT103 using the exact legal name of the CK_IC and a unique remittance reference such as 'CAP-INJ-2025-001'; (2) use ISO 20022 purpose code 'CAPT' (capital transfer) for subscribed share capital or 'LIMA' (loan in) for shareholder loans, ensuring the payment narrative matches the underlying corporate transaction to prevent false matching with the registered agent's omnibus account; (3) deliver to the bank, before or simultaneously with the wire, a board resolution of the CK_IC approving the capital increase or loan drawdown, the subscription agreement, and the executed shareholder loan agreement; (4) for recurring US-client retainer income received via 'Retainer_ACH', the US correspondent bank of the NZ receiving bank will pass the ACH credit to the IC's ASB or Airwallex virtual USD account, with the NACHA entry description appearing as 'PR Retainer' and the merchant legal name of the IC; (5) upon arrival, apply a pre-arranged auto-sweep spot FX instruction to convert surplus USD into NZD at the daily interbank rate, or park USD in the FCY account pending disbursement timing; (6) any single inbound wire exceeding NZD 50,000 equivalent should be accompanied by a source-of-funds declaration in the bank's prescribed format; and (7) all inbound capital must be disclosed under the overseas investment, CRS/FATCA, and, where applicable, the New Zealand controlled foreign company rules when the shareholder is an NZ tax resident.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary rail: SWIFT MT103 (gpi) for all invoice payments to overseas PR partners, sub-agencies, media buying platforms, and freelance contractors; each MT103 carries purpose code 'SERV' (payment of services) plus the supplier's invoice number and the IC's internal purchase identifier, and is routed through the bank's global payments innovation tracking chain for same-day or next-day credit. For large recurring media-buy settlements exceeding USD 250,000 equivalent per month, the recommended rail is a Commercial Letter of Credit governed by UCP600 issued by Westpac New Zealand Limited in favour of the media supplier, payable against presentation of a signed proof-of-performance certificate, commercial invoice, and customs or broadcast-affidavit documentation; alternatively, a standby LC can be used to underpin a netting agreement with a preferred media vendor. For domestic New Zealand payments to NZ-based reporters, production houses, and legal counsel, use BECS (Bulk Electronic Clearing System) with the standard three-settlement-day calendar for NZD. For US-dollar payments to US vendors and media platforms, either (i) the US correspondent bank's Fedwire channel, or (ii) the US ACH network for lower-value recurring disbursements under the 'Retainer_ACH' symmetrical payment pattern. Treasury best practice: establish a same-day multi-currency netting protocol that offsets USD retainer receivables against USD supplier payables before any FX conversion, and maintain a one-touch settlement calendar covering retainer collection dates, supplier invoice deadlines, and the bank's FX fixing windows.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright deliverable FX forward (NZD/USD, NZD/AUD, NZD/EUR) with tenors up to 12 months, executed on a relationship basis under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with the settling New Zealand bank, available for hedging the USD-denominated PR retainer income stream.

Non-deliverable forward (NDF) on restricted Asian currencies (including IDR, PHP, VND, MYR, KRW, and TWD) where the PR agency pays sub-agents or media suppliers in a currency that is not fully deliverable offshore, with the NZD/USD margin leg settled in NZD on an agreed fixing date.

Cross-currency swap (NZD/USD and NZD/EUR) for large multi-year global retainer contracts, converting a substantial fixed-USD receivable stream into floating or fixed NZD funding for the operational entity.
Vanilla FX put options (purchase-only, no writing) to cap the downside of adverse NZD/USD movement on major campaign retainer receipts, with the net premium capped at 150 basis points per annum.

Short-term NZD/USD FX swap for treasury-liquidity bridging between the moment of US ACH retainer collection and the monthly settlement cycle of outbound trade disbursements, thereby eliminating intraday currency exposure and settlement risk.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return and Government Renewal Fee (Cook Islands International Companies Act)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of International Companies, Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission (Realm of New Zealand)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 days after each anniversary of incorporation; annual government fee is payable by the anniversary date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late fee accrues for overdue annual return or fee; after formal notice and continued default, the Registrar may administratively strike the company off and dissolve it.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Beneficial Ownership Confirmation / Register Update
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission (submitted through the licensed registered agent)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually with the annual return; beneficial ownership changes must be notified to the registered agent within 14 days of the change
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Non-compliance may trigger statutory penalties, prevent issuance of a certificate of good standing, and support administrative strike-off for serious or repeated default.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No compulsory audit threshold applies to an ordinary International Company. Mandatory audit applies only to licensed international banking, trust, insurance, or other regulated entities, or where shareholders, the board, court, or Registrar requires an audit.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS as a recognized reporting framework; for voluntarily prepared unaudited financial statements, the board may adopt IFRS or US GAAP with disclosure of the framework applied.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Before the annual return anniversary, the registered agent must obtain a current beneficial ownership schedule and a written directors' representation confirming that the UBO register is accurate and complete; share transfers during the year must be recorded in the register and notified to the registered agent within 14 days.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Members (shareholders and share transfers)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 800 - USD 1,800 (licensed registered agent and registered office, inclusive of standard corporate secretarial services)
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: Not statutorily required for an ordinary International Company; voluntary certified audit, if commissioned, generally USD 7,500 - USD 18,000

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general statutory tax holidays. Standard corporate tax rate of 28% applies to all resident companies. A non-resident company that is not resident in New Zealand for tax purposes is generally not subject to New Zealand income tax on foreign-sourced income. Certain limited tax incentives exist, such as the loss attributing qualifying company (LAQC) regime for qualifying companies and the research and development tax credit of 15% for eligible R&D expenditure. However, an International Company (IC) structured as an offshore non-resident-owned entity deriving only foreign-sourced income would typically have no New Zealand taxable income and no effective tax rate. For a New Zealand-resident PR agency, the standard 28% rate applies with no preferential deduction beyond ordinary business deductions.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: New Zealand Inland Revenue (IR) income tax return form IR4 for companies, filed electronically via myIR (IR's secure online portal). Non-resident companies may file form IR4 with supplementary schedules as applicable. Exceptional non-resident filers with limited New Zealand source income may use IR3 or specific non-resident filing schedules as directed by IR.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The tax return and payment are due by the 7th day of the month following the end of the company's balance date. For a standard 31 March balance date, the return is due 7 July. Terminal tax and provisional tax instalments follow the IR's instalment schedule; for a March balance date, terminal tax is due 7 July. If the company uses a different balance date, the corresponding 7th day of the following month applies. A company with no New Zealand taxable income and classified as a non-resident foreign company may have a nil filing obligation but must consider whether it is required to register with Inland Revenue and file a return if it carries on a taxable activity in New Zealand or derives New Zealand-sourced income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Statement of Accounts / Financial Statements
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Full income statement and balance sheet extracted from IFRS-compliant financial statements, including turnover, cost of sales, operating expenses, taxable income, and tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident PR agency: report only New Zealand-sourced gross income and deductible expenses attributable to that New Zealand-sourced business. Foreign-sourced income of a non-resident company is not assessable. Attach New Zealand branch financial accounts if a fixed establishment or agency exists. If no New Zealand source income, state nil and confirm no taxable activity.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total assessable income after exclusion of exempt income and non-assessable foreign income. Includes gross dividends and interest derived from New Zealand sources.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident filer: enter only gross New Zealand-sourced income. Exclude all offshore retainer income, foreign royalties, and foreign interest. If loss-attributing or conduit wholly owned group treatment elected, follow applicable attribution rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: All deductible business expenses incurred in deriving assessable income, including overhead allocation, personnel costs, office rent, professional fees, and depreciation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident filer: claim only expenses attributable to New Zealand-source income. Apportion global overhead on a fair and reasonable basis consistent with transfer pricing standards. Do not deduct head office charges or global brand costs that are not incurred for the New Zealand branch.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Box 3: Net taxable income / loss
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income after deducting expenses and applying tax adjustments, such as depreciation adjustments, timing differences, and disallowable expenditure.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Compute net taxable income solely from New Zealand-source activity. A loss may arise only if deductible NZ-source expenses exceed NZ-source income. Foreign losses of a non-resident are not deductible. Resident IC companies with only foreign income should report nil and submit a loss or nil return if required.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income tax payable computed at 28% of net taxable income, reduced by available tax credits, RWT credits, foreign tax credits, and imputation credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident: apply 28% to NZ-source net taxable income only. Claim New Zealand dividends imputation credits or resident withholding tax credits on NZ-source interest/dividends. Do not claim foreign tax credits unless a New Zealand-resident company with foreign-source income taxed in New Zealand, which does not apply to a non-resident IC deriving solely foreign income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Box 5: Imputation credit account / Supplementary schedule
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Record of New Zealand dividends paid and imputation credits attached, if any distribution was made by a New Zealand-resident company.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident companies without New Zealand residency do not maintain an imputation credit account. If treated as a New Zealand resident and paying dividends, attach Schedule 8 (imputation return) and attach imputation credits in accordance with corporate tax law.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: IR4 – Box 6: Provisional tax paid / terminal tax
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Amount of provisional tax instalments already paid and resulting terminal tax payable or refund due.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident: if the company has a New Zealand fixed establishment and derives assessable NZ income, provisional tax applies. If no NZ-source income and no fixed establishment, no provisional tax obligations. Terminal tax due date aligns with 7th day of month following balance date.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: immediate late filing penalty of NZ$250 for IR4 companies. Subsequent annual penalties apply based on outstanding tax. Late payment penalties: 1% of unpaid tax on the day after the due date and an additional 2% if not paid within 7 days. An incremental penalty of 1% for each further month or part-month that the tax remains unpaid, capped at 10% total monthly penalty. Use-of-money interest (UOMI) for companies is charged on unpaid provisional/terminal tax at the prescribed rate (currently around 8.68% per annum for underpayments, adjusted quarterly). Non-filing of a return when required also constitutes an offence under the Tax Administration Act 1994, subject to a maximum fine of NZ$25,000 for a company, and possible further penalties for knowingly providing false returns or evading tax up to 200% of the tax avoided plus criminal sanctions including imprisonment up to 5 years.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: New Zealand's statutory non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) rate on gross dividends paid by a New Zealand-resident company to a non-resident shareholder is 30% unless reduced under an applicable double tax agreement (DTA). No NRWT is imposed on dividends paid by a Non-resident International Company that is not a New Zealand tax resident and derives no New Zealand-source income, as no New Zealand dividend is deemed to occur in the New Zealand tax system.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: A non-resident shareholder must claim treaty relief by completing the relevant Inland Revenue form (IR290 – Certificate of Rate of Non-Resident Withholding Tax for a particular country, or IR291 – Certificate of Rate of NRWT for companies) and providing it to the New Zealand payer before payment of the dividend, interest, or royalty. The certificate must be accompanied by a valid tax residency certificate (TRC) issued by the shareholder's residence jurisdiction for the relevant income year, evidencing treaty residence and beneficial ownership. The New Zealand payer applies the reduced treaty rate by withholding at the reduced rate at the time of payment. A refund of excess NRWT may be claimed where withholding occurred at the full rate and the certificate is later obtained; the claim is made through an IR refund application or amended schedule, subject to the four-year statutory time bar. The OECD Model-based DTA provisions generally require the shareholder to be the beneficial owner, satisfy any limitation of benefits clause, and have no permanent establishment in New Zealand to which the dividend is effectively connected. Active business income paid to a New Zealand branch of the shareholder cannot be subject to final NRWT and instead is taxed as part of the branch profits under the corporate rate.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory NRWT: 15% for royalties and interest paid by a New Zealand-resident company to a non-resident (if not subject to certain exemptions such as approved issuer levies). The approved issuer levy (AIL) regime provides that interest paid to a non-resident on approved convertible or other eligible debt securities may be subject to a 2% levy instead of NRWT if the New Zealand borrower is an approved issuer and the lender does not have a controlling relationship. Treaty rates: The New Zealand–China DTA (relevant to the sovereign context of a parent holding company in the People's Republic of China) reduces interest withholding to 10% (or 0% where the interest is paid to a financial institution/bank and meets specified conditions) and royalties to 10%. Some other treaties, e.g. New Zealand–Australia and New Zealand–United States, have 0% or 10% rates on interest and generally 5% or 10% on royalties depending on type of intellectual property. A shareholdingholding condition for dividend treaty rates commonly reduces the 30% statutory rate to 15% for portfolio holdings and to 5% for companies holding at least 10% of the voting power (under most New Zealand treaties). The protocol to claim treaty relief requires the recipient to be resident in the treaty jurisdiction, beneficial owner, and subject to an active trade or business test for certain business income exemptions. RoyaltiesTax withholding applies to payments for the use of, or right to use, any copyright, trademark, patent, design, secret formula, or process, including fees for the supply of commercial information. The 15% statutory rate applies unless the relevant DTA reduces it. For the cross-border PR communication firm, royalty payments for the use of global brand names, client databases, or proprietary media monitoring software may incur NRWT at the applicable rate if sourced in New Zealand; conversely, royalties paid by the offshore entity to New Zealand residents for New Zealand-developed intellectual property may be subject to New Zealand's foreign-source royalty rules only if the percentage of income derived from New Zealand exceeds a threshold under section CC 7-8 of the Income Tax Act 2007.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand's transfer pricing rules apply to cross-border related-party transactions where the New Zealand entity and the foreign entity are associated persons. There is no monetary threshold below which transfer pricing documentation is exempt, but administrative penalties can be neutralised where taxpayers prepare contemporaneous documentation. Inland Revenue's transfer pricing Guidelines require: (i) functional analysis, (ii) economic analysis, (iii) selection of the most appropriate transfer pricing method, and (iv) documentation maintained before the return is filed. The OECD Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) threshold requires a New Zealand-resident ultimate parent of a multinational group with consolidated group revenue of NZ$1.05 billion or more (approximately EUR 750 million under the OECD aligned threshold) to file a CbCR. The local entity of a qualifying MNE group must file a notification (IR402) and may be required to file a Master File and Local File. Although the CbCR threshold is NZ$1.05 billion, a mid-sized PR firm controlled by an offshore parent is unlikely to exceed it, but all related-party cross-border payments, including management fees, service fees, intellectual property royalties, and intercompany loans, must satisfy the arm's length standard regardless of size. New Zealand's transfer pricing penalty regime: where a transfer pricing adjustment arises, a shortfall penalty of 20% of the tax shortfall applies if the taxpayer did not take reasonable care, and 40% if the adjustment exceeds NZ$250,000 or the dominant purpose is tax avoidance. A 100% penalty may apply for evasion. The safe harbour for certain cross-border lease transactions has no general application to intra-group services. International Company entities registered as non-resident foreign companies should not maintain a New Zealand permanent establishment in order to avoid New Zealand transfer pricing and income tax obligations; however, if the IC has a New Zealand-resident director or an agency in New Zealand that habitually concludes contracts, a PE risk arises, requiring full transfer pricing documentation and income attribution.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand is not a jurisdiction that maintains formal Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) in the manner of the Caribbean/offshore ESR regimes enacted after the EU Code of Conduct Group. However, New Zealand's substantive tax law and the OECD's BEPS agenda impose anti-avoidance principles and general anti-avoidance rules (GAAR) under section BG 1 Income Tax Act 2007, and the 'economic substance' concept appears in: (1) the offshore international company exemption from New Zealand taxing jurisdiction where the company is non-resident and has no fixed establishment in New Zealand, but if such company is centrally managed and controlled in New Zealand it becomes resident and fully taxable; (2) New Zealand's controlled foreign company (CFC) rules and foreign investment fund (FIF) rules; (3) thin capitalisation rules for residents and non-residents with excess debt; and (4) the substantial business presence exception for hybrid mismatch and permanent establishment attribution. For an International Company (IC) structured as an offshore PR communication firm, both the Cook Islands International Company regime (where the entity is likely resident) and New Zealand tax law require that the entity demonstrates real substantive presence in its claimed jurisdiction of tax residence, including physical office, employees who conduct core income-generating activities (signing client contracts, executing campaigns, handling media relationships), local discretion over fees and budgets, bank accounts, and adequate records. A pure 'mailbox' entity registered in the Cook Islands or other tax-neutral jurisdiction but administered from New Zealand would be deemed a New Zealand resident under case law applying the central management and control test, causing full New Zealand taxation on worldwide income and application of the same GAAR. The Cook Islands International Companies Act provides that an international company has no tax liability on international income and no requirement to maintain financial records locally, but this exemption does not override New Zealand's resident tax jurisdiction where management and control are exercised in New Zealand. The New Zealand IRD actively applies the 'creation of value' analysis to determine economic substance and has the power to assess a person as having a permanent establishment in New Zealand if there is a fixed place in New Zealand through which the business of the non-resident is wholly or partly carried on, or if an agent in New Zealand habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts in the name of the non-resident.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately understating New Zealand-source income, claiming deductions for unrelated offshore expenses, shifting profits to a tax-haven International Company without actual transfer of functions, personnel, risks, or assets, or using a shell entity to conceal a PE in New Zealand. Arrangements whose purpose is to defeat the intent and application of the Income Tax Act 2007 trigger the general anti-avoidance rule (section BG 1). This includes round-trip financing, excessive royalties, artificial intercompany service fees, or creating a non-resident 'controller' that is in substance a New Zealand-resident decision-maker.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Tax Administration Act 1994, a tax shortfall arising from an avoidance arrangement is subject to a penalty of 20% (not reasonably arguable position) or 40% (dominant purpose of tax avoidance) of the shortfall. Evasion is subject to a 100% penalty. Late payment penalties and use-of-money interest accrue at up to 10% per month. Criminal prosecution can result in a fine of up to NZ$50,000 for a company and up to NZ$50,000 against an individual plus imprisonment of up to 5 years for tax evasion or knowingly providing false returns. For severe cases of fraud, the Crimes Act 1961 penalties apply. Inland Revenue also has the power to issue a 'notice to produce documents' and conduct dawn raids under judicial warrants.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be held personally liable for tax shortfalls where they are involved in the preparation of false documents or knowingly participate in evasion. The veil of incorporation may be pierced under the Companies Act 1993, the Tax Administration Act 1994, and the Financial Markets Conduct Act where the company is used as a sham or façade to conceal illegality. Directors may be liable for civil penalties equal to the amount of tax not withheld under the PAYE and RWT regimes (director penalties), plus interest and penalties. Travel restrictions may be imposed by the District Court at the request of Inland Revenue to prevent departure from New Zealand when taxes are outstanding; commercial or personal assets may be restrained or forfeited under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009. Directors who breach their duties by allowing the company to trade while insolvent may face personal liability for unpaid tax and for reckless trading under the Company Act. Imprisonment applies where evasion is proven, and directors may be disqualified from managing companies for up to 5 years.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Maintaining an empty International Company in a zero-tax jurisdiction (e.g., Cook Islands IC registry) with no genuine office, employees, decision-making, or business activity, while the real PR communication services are performed by staff in New Zealand. Using the offshore entity to issue invoices for revenue, hold IP without development, and avoid New Zealand income tax. The Inland Revenue may determine the offshore entity's income is attributable to a New Zealand permanent establishment or to the New Zealand-resident company under transfer pricing recharacterisation and attribution of profit rules.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Reclassification of the offshore entity as a New Zealand tax resident or as a PE of the offshore entity results in a full assessment of New Zealand corporate tax at 28% on profits, plus NRWT on any deemed distributions. Penalties for an avoidance arrangement or evasion range from 20% to 100% of the shortfall, plus use-of-money interest. If a company is found to be a 'shell' for tax purposes, Inland Revenue may also impose non-filing penalties and administrative penalties of NZ$250 for each late return. More broadly, the entity could be struck off the New Zealand Companies Register if considered non-compliant, and if registered overseas as an IC, the relevant international company registry may impose fines for failure to file annual declarations of a paid registered agent (typically ranging from US$100 to US$1,000 depending on the jurisdiction).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly operate a shell company as a tax avoidance vehicle are joint and several liability with the company for the tax shortfall. Under the Tax Administration Act 1994, they can be made personally liable for penalties and interest. In criminal proceedings, directors face imprisonment of up to 5 years and fines of up to NZ$50,000. International travel by directors can be restricted through a departure prohibition order where tax is unpaid. Personal assets can be pursued in civil recovery, and directors may be liable under the Companies Act for allowing the business to carry on with the intent to defraud creditors (fraudulent trading) or reckless trading. The New Zealand Directors' duties under the Companies Act 1993 (sections 135-137) require care, diligence, and prudent business judgment; a director of a foreign IC managing operations from New Zealand cannot ignore liability by pleading lack of local director status, as the place of effective management is New Zealand.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the overseas PR communication firm to process retainer ACH payments or wire transfers that conceal the true beneficiary, or receiving payments from politically exposed persons (PEPs) or sanctioned jurisdictions in connection with PR/crisis communications without conducting customer due diligence, ongoing CDD, or filing suspicious transaction reports. Although the entity is a 'Low_Risk_Standard' banking AML tier and not a statutorily licensed financial institution in New Zealand, a professional service firm that invoices on behalf of clients or moves funds in a way that circumvents AML/CFT obligations of banks may be caught by the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 if it engages in a financial activity specified under that Act. Operating shell bank accounts, accepting cash deposits without origin, or creating layered wire transfers across multiple jurisdictions to obscure origins or recipients constitutes money laundering or terrorist financing support.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the AML/CFT Act 2009, reporting entities failing to carry out CDD or KYC procedures are liable to civil penalties up to NZ$200,000 for an individual and NZ$2,000,000 for a company per contravention; significant contraventions may be up to NZ$400,000 and NZ$4,000,000 for companies. Money laundering itself is an offence under the Crimes Act 1961 (section 243), carrying a maximum sentence of 7 years' imprisonment for natural persons and unlimited fines for companies. Financing of terrorism is punishable by imprisonment of up to 14 years (Crimes Act 1961, sections 244-245 and Terrorism Suppression Act 2002). For arranging or facilitating transactions involving a designated terrorist entity, conviction can lead to 7 years to 14 years imprisonment. For shell companies controlling financial accounts, the court may order criminal forfeiture of the funds and assets involved, up to the full value, under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009; a restraint order or asset freezing order may be issued immediately. The Financial Markets Authority (FMA) can suspend the entity's ability to transact through the New Zealand banking system.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior managers can be personally prosecuted for AML/CFT offences if they authorised, participated in, or failed to prevent the offending. They face imprisonment of up to 7 years for laundering and up to 14 years for terrorist financing; fines of up to NZ$2,000,000 per contravention for the entity and individual liability for compensation orders. Directors' and officers' insurance does not cover criminal conduct. A director of a non-resident IC with New Zealand management who is found guilty of money laundering also automatically faces seizure of personal assets, travel bans under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act, and prohibition from being a director of any New Zealand company or managed entity. New Zealand Police can issue a 'production order' requiring a corporate service provider to disclose the director's identity, and the director may be extradited depending on bilateral treaties between New Zealand and the IC's registry jurisdiction in the Cook Islands.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The offshore parent or IC charges a New Zealand branch or New Zealand client through artificial intercompany invoices for services that are not actually rendered, excessive management fees, marketing royalty payments for international 'reputation' or brand rights, or interest on a loan that is not a genuine debt obligation. Failing to maintain contemporaneous documentation, functional analysis, and comparable benchmarking for cross-border controlled transactions; using a TNMM profit margin that does not reflect the PR industry's normal operating margins; or stripping profits out of New Zealand via intercompany payables without adding value.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Inland Revenue may make a transfer pricing adjustment, imputing a commercially realistic arm's length profit to the New Zealand company. The adjusted taxable income is taxed at 28%, and a shortfall penalty of 20% applies where the taxpayer did not adopt a reasonably arguable position; 40% where the adjustment exceeds NZ$250,000 or the arrangement's dominant purpose is tax avoidance. Evasion adds a 100% penalty. Interest accrues from return due date. In addition, unpaid withholding tax on interest/royalties (NRWT 15% or 2% AIL) is assessed, plus penalties of 10% per month. The dividend may be recharacterised as a dividend, giving rise to NRWT of 30% or applicable treaty rate. The CbCR and Country-by-Country reporting notification failure can result in penalties of NZ$50,000 per entity per year plus NZ$10,000 per month continued.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: A director who signs incorrect transfer pricing documentation or assists in creating false intercompany agreements is personally exposed to civil penalties for aiding and abetting tax evasion. Personal liability for a company's tax debt may arise under the 'director penalty' regime for unpaid PAYE/RWT, and for other taxes where reckless behaviour is proven. Courts may pierce the corporate veil to recover unpaid tax where there is evidence of fraud, irregularity, or the company being an instrument of its director. Indictment for tax evasion committed as an associated enterprise could result in imprisonment. Travel restrictions are available where tax is unpaid and a director attempts to leave New Zealand.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Breach of Statutory Return Obligations / Non-Compliance with IC Registry Filings
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to file annual returns or notifications in both New Zealand (if taxable activity or PE exists) and the Cook Islands International Company registry, failure to pay the annual registered agent fee, failure to keep accounting records for the minimum statutory period, or failure to notify Inland Revenue of a disqualifying event such as change in directors, termination of the New Zealand resident agent, or cessation of the foreign trust's underlying business.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: In New Zealand: late filing penalty of NZ$250 per return, automatic late payment penalty of 1% plus 2% additional penalty, incremental monthly penalties up to 10%, use-of-money interest. Failure to provide requested documents can draw penalties of NZ$2,000 per month per document under the Tax Administration Act, up to NZ$50,000. In the Cook Islands: annual company licensing fees are assessed for late penalty, and a company in default of its annual license return is subject to a fine of up to NZ$500 plus the loss of its international company status; continued default may result in strike-off and the company's assets vesting in the Cook Islands government. However, the New Zealand-controlled 'IC' structure may face a reclassification as a New Zealand resident if it is not actually managed and controlled in the Cook Islands, and any representation that the entity is 'tax exempt' while operating from New Zealand is fraudulent.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are personally liable for filing fees and penalties in the Cook Islands, and the Cook Islands Financial Intelligence Unit can impose AML penalties. In New Zealand, a director who fails to ensure timely filing of tax returns is subject to director penalty assessments under the Tax Administration Act, equal to the unpaid tax amount plus interest. A director who permits a company to be struck off while outstanding tax liabilities exist can be personally liable for unpaid debts. Under the Companies Act, a director who fails to comply with record-keeping obligations commits an offence, punishable by a fine of up to NZ$200,000, and an individual can be disqualified. Travel bans may be issued under Inland Revenue's Tax Recovery enforcement, potentially for unlimited duration until tax payable is settled, as well as a court-ordered sale of assets.
